messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Vignette:
Leela's eyes still scan every room she enters, a habit formed in the months following her escape from her abusive partner. She'll catch glimpses of herself in mirrors and windows, checking for any signs of distress or vulnerability. As a tutor, she works with students in their homes, but she can't shake off the feeling that danger lurks around every corner. Her hyper-vigilance towards people has become so ingrained that she finds it difficult to relax, even when surrounded by familiar faces. The memories of the physical abuse still haunt her in fragmented pieces - a shattered vase here, a slammed door there, the sound of her partner's voice raised in anger. When these disjointed recollections surface, Leela is transported back to the terror she felt during those moments. The images are so vivid that it's as if she's looking at photographs - frozen in time, yet still radiating fear. Leela has come to believe that she's permanently changed for the worse. She feels like an outsider now, someone who can no longer trust her own instincts or sense of safety. Her partner's abuse had eroded her confidence, leaving her with a deep-seated fear of harm. You can never know who will harm you, Leela tells herself, and this mantra has become her reality. Her body often reacts before her mind has time to process the threat - a sudden noise, a raised voice, or an unexpected movement sends her heart racing. She's constantly on guard, her senses heightened as she searches for potential dangers in any environment. Even innocuous objects can be perceived as threats: a sharp edge on a table, a heavy bookend, or a stray screwdriver. Leela's hypervigilance has started to affect her relationships with others. Her students' parents have begun to notice that she seems distracted and preoccupied during sessions. Her own husband feels like he's walking on eggshells around her, never knowing what might trigger another panic episode. Leela knows that she needs help, but the thought of confronting her past traumas is daunting. As a tutor, Leela had always prided herself on being able to create a safe and nurturing environment for her students. Now, she feels like she's lost that ability - and with it, a part of herself. She hopes that seeking therapy will help her rebuild her sense of self-worth and learn to navigate the world without constantly feeling on edge. What brought her to this point was a recent incident where one of her students accidentally knocked over a bookshelf, causing Leela to have a full-blown panic attack. It was then that she realized she couldn't continue living like this - trapped in a state of perpetual fear and hypervigilance.
